Package com.stzteam.features.robotlocalization.vio.sim

Class VioErrorModel

java.lang.Object
com.stzteam.features.robotlocalization.vio.sim.VioErrorModel
public class VioErrorModel extends Object
The visual-inertial odometry error model. It is the real content of this feature.

A Limelight either sees the tag or it does not. A Quest always reports a pose; what changes is how much it lies. Simulating the protocol without simulating the lie would give a perfect sensor, which is exactly the one nobody needs to test against.

Continuous drift

The drift scales with distance travelled, not with time: a stationary robot does not drift, and one crossing the field does. That is how real VIO behaves. The yaw drifts with accumulated rotation, for the same reason.

Failure modes

The four QuestNav documents, each injectable from the Sim GUI or from a test:
  • Feature loss (low light, reflections, uniform surfaces). The documentation says the Quest may re-acquire tracking with an offset, so when it recovers the pose comes back displaced. That jump is what breaks a finely tuned pose estimator.
  • Vibration-induced double-tap to passthrough: a pose discontinuity without losing tracking. More treacherous, because isTracking stays true.
  • Critical battery: the headset shuts itself off mid-match.
  • Network drop: publishing stops and isConnected() falls after 120 ms.

The last two are not pose error but absence of data, so SimulatedQuestNav handles them by consulting isPoweredOn() and isLinkUp(double).

About the default values

They are plausible, not measured. They are chosen so the order of magnitude is reasonable and so the failures show up within a short test. If you have logs from your own headset, tune them.

A deliberate simplification

Position drift and yaw drift are modelled as additive and independent. In a real VIO the heading error also curves the estimated trajectory. Reproducing that would require dragging a drifting reference frame around, and for this feature's purpose --- breaking a pose estimator realistically --- it changes nothing: what matters is that the error grows with distance travelled, that it jumps on re-acquisition, and that a POSE_RESET clears it.

    • update

      public edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Pose3d update(edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Pose3d truePose, double nowSeconds, double dtSeconds)
      Advances the model one step and returns the pose the headset should report.
      Parameters:
      truePose - the headset's real pose (robot + mount), according to the simulation.
      nowSeconds - the current instant, in FPGA seconds.
      dtSeconds - time elapsed since the previous call.
      Returns:
      the pose with the error applied. If tracking is lost, the frozen pose.

      public void injectTrackingLoss(double durationSeconds, double nowSeconds)
      Forces a tracking loss. On recovery, the pose comes back displaced.
      Parameters:
      durationSeconds - how long the loss lasts.
      nowSeconds - the current instant, in FPGA seconds.

    • injectPoseDiscontinuity

      public void injectPoseDiscontinuity(edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Translation3d jump)
      Injects a pose discontinuity without losing tracking. It reproduces the double-tap to passthrough that chassis vibration triggers: isTracking stays true, so the robot code has no way of knowing the pose has just jumped.
      Parameters:
      jump - the displacement to apply, in metres.

    • resetDrift

      public void resetDrift()
      Clears the accumulated drift. The POSE_RESET handler calls it, because a real reset re-anchors the headset's origin and leaves the error at zero.
